Most manuscripts, nearly all of them later, go on with 16:9-20, the longer ending. Its style and vocabulary differ from the rest of Mark: many of its words occur nowhere else in the Gospel, it introduces Mary Magdalene in 16:9 as if she had not just been named in 16:1, and its appearances read like a summary of those told in Luke, John and Acts. Some manuscripts have instead a short ending after 16:8 (the women report briefly to Peter's companions, and Jesus sends out through them the proclamation of eternal salvation), and a few have the short ending followed by the longer one. old: Whether Mark meant to end at 16:8 or his first ending was lost is an open question. A book ending on the word "for", with the women silent and afraid, is very unusual, and it leaves the meeting promised in 16:7 untold. Some think the last page of the earliest copy was lost or never written. Others think Mark ended here on purpose: the promise of 16:7 stands, the reader knows the message was later told, and the silence leaves the reader facing the empty tomb. The later endings show that early copyists felt the Gospel needed a fuller close. The manuscripts cannot settle the question. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

old: The story of the woman caught in adultery is missing from the earliest manuscripts of John, among them two early papyri (P66 and P75), Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and from the early versions in other ancient languages. The first manuscript known to have it is Codex Bezae, from the fifth century. In later manuscripts it is found here, but some place it after John 7:36, after 7:44 or at the end of the Gospel after 21:25, and one group places it in Luke, after Luke 21:38. Some manuscripts that have it mark it as doubtful. Its style and vocabulary differ from the rest of John: it names the scribes (verse 3) and the Mount of Olives (8:1), which John does not otherwise mention, and uses other words John rarely uses. Many hold that it is an old and true account of Jesus that was handed down outside John and later written into the Gospel at this point. The SBLGNT prints it here in double brackets. It is translated here in square brackets: the opening bracket at the start of 7:53 and the closing bracket at the end of 8:11 mark where the passage begins and ends. The evidence shows that the passage was not part of the earliest copies of John; it does not decide whether the events took place. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

new: Manuscripts end Romans in different ways. Many later manuscripts repeat the blessing of verse 20 here as verse 24; the oldest leave it out. The doxology (the closing praise to God traditionally numbered 16:25-27) stands after 16:23 in the oldest manuscripts, after 14:23 in many later ones, after 15:33 in the oldest papyrus, in two places in some, and is missing in a few. The SBLGNT data this project pins prints verse 24, marked as a place where manuscripts differ, and has no 16:25-27; the doxology is translated in the next record (16:25-27) from the Nestle 1904 text. The SBLGNT apparatus shows that the SBLGNT prints verse 24 with the Robinson-Pierpont Byzantine text, while Westcott and Hort, Tregelles and NA28 leave it out and print 16:25-27 at this point. new: The SBLGNT data this project pins has no 16:25-27, so these three verses, and only these, are translated from the Nestle 1904 Greek text (MACULA Greek's Nestle 1904 data), which prints them after 16:23-24.
